title: Catching drinking water out of the air
bodyMd: In the hills above the coastal town of Cerro Alto, thick fog rolls inland on most mornings, but almost no rain falls. Hydrologist Nadia Belmont strings vertical mesh nets across the ridge: droplets carried in the fog catch on the threads, run down into a gutter and collect in a tank. Belmont's first nets used a very fine weave, on the reasoning that a denser mesh would intercept more droplets. In practice those nets performed worst of all. Air could not pass through them, so each bank of fog was pushed around the net rather than through it, and the droplets travelled with it. A coarser mesh, which slowed the air without blocking it, yielded nearly three times as much water per day.
accessibilityText: A short science passage. Above the coastal town of Cerro Alto, thick fog arrives most mornings but almost no rain falls. Hydrologist Nadia Belmont hangs vertical mesh nets across the ridge so that fog droplets catch on the threads, run into a gutter and collect in a tank. Her first nets used a very fine weave because she reasoned that a denser mesh would intercept more droplets. Those fine nets performed worst of all, because air could not pass through them, so the fog was pushed around the net instead of through it and carried its droplets away. A coarser mesh that slowed the air without blocking it produced nearly three times as much water per day.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item bank. Cerro Alto, the hydrologist and the three-times figure are invented; fog-net water collection is described only in general terms and no published text was consulted or adapted.
